newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers made inroads, but budget deal elusive.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers made inroads, but budget deal elusive.

text.p: European Union finance ministers on Monday edged closer to clinching a deal to keep budget spending on a tight rein after monetary union starts, but said they must meet again to thrash out remaining differences.
The ministers said they would reconvene on December 12 in Dublin, on the eve of a summit meeting of EU leaders, in the hope that a deal could be put on the table at the meeting.
"There is a will and a desire to make considerable progress in Dublin...We want a proper agreement," Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, who currently chairs the ECOFIN council, said.
British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said an agreement on crucial issues dividing the ministers had been only just out of reach.
"We were quite close to an agreement, but we were not quite able to reach it," he told reporters after the talks broke up around 2045 GMT.
Earlier, the ministers had looked increasingly close to cementing a crucial agreement on the fiscal discipline plan.
"They are in the box," one diplomat told Reuters, referring to the various elements of the proposed stability pact between EU member states.
"For the first time there is a deep discussion on all the aspects," a second diplomat said.

But the talks nonetheless remained deadlocked on several key points of the planned pact -- proposed by German finance minister Theo Waigel to make sure that a future single currency is not undermined by excessive government spending.

Above all, they had proved unable to agree a definition of "exceptional and temporary" economic circumstances which would allow a country's budget deficit to exceed an agreed upper limit of three percent of its gross domestic product.

Germany, supported by the Netherlands, has been insistent that there must be a strict, numerical definition of such circumstances, fearing that any other option could pave the way for political fudging which would weaken the pact.
Diplomats said that breakthrough on this appeared to have been triggered by a presidency proposal on a definition of these exceptional circumstances.
The presidency had suggested as a compromise definition of "significantly negative growth" adding that this would have to be supported by additional evidence, they said.

Other diplomats said that Waigel, still keen to have a numerical definition of the exceptional conditions, was now looking to set this at a contraction in gross domestic product for four consecutive quarters or 1.5 percent in total in a year.

Going into the meeting, Germany had been demanding that an unusually strong recession be defined as a contraction of two percent in gross domestic product. The European Commission, backed by several countries, had not wanted any figure to be specified.
But Waigel's concession clearly did not go far enough for full agreement to be reached.

Clarke, in an apparent reference to Waigel, commented, "I do think it is a relatively minor point. But there are people... who want definitions that are extremely narrow and defining." He declined to name names.
But diplomats said that even with the sticky issue of definitions outstanding, there had been some progress in setting the level of fines an offending country would face.

The ministers had apparently agreed to a fixed level of fine which countries would face if they overshot the maximum permitted level. The initial fine would be 0.2 percent of GDP, rising to a maximum of 0.5 percent, the diplomats said.
